word_order: SVO | Example sentences show canonical Subject–Verb–Object order (e.g. 'Steve Jobs unveiled the device', 'Mutations can have a variety of different effects').
register: edited written informational prose (news, encyclopedia, technical/descriptive writing), not spontaneous dialogue.
discourse_markers: coordinating conjunctions for linking clauses (and, but)
subordinating/concessive markers introducing dependent clauses (although, because, if, while)
sentence-level adverbial/linking phrases (in the end, of course, following)
clause_boundary_signals: subordinating conjunctions/complementizers that introduce a clause (although, because, if)
relative/complementizer pronouns introducing embedded clauses (who, that, which)
coordinating conjunctions often accompanied by a pause/comma when joining clauses (and, but)
non_boundary_traps: non-restrictive appositives/parenthetical inserts set off by commas (e.g. 'live on television')
prepositional phrases or temporal adverbials that can appear clause-initial but attach to verb or noun (e.g. 'For over a thousand years', 'After the war')
reduced/non-finite participial modifiers that look like separate actions but modify a noun or clause (e.g. 'breaking the previous record')
noun-modifying 'of'-phrases and numeric quantifiers that form long noun groups (e.g. 'Eighteen percent of Venezuelans')
unstable_prefix_signals: sentence-initial subordinators or adverbial prepositional phrases (although, because of, after, following) after which the eventual clause type or scope can still be reversed by following material
ambiguous clause-openers that can be temporal or concessive (while, as)
notes_for_prompt_writer: The language is English with canonical SVO order and frequent use of auxiliary verbs and negation on auxiliaries (will set, had been nationalised, aren't trusted). Sentential structure commonly includes subordinating conjunctions and relative/complementizer pronouns to introduce embedded clauses. Many modifiers are multiword (prepositional phrases, 'of'-phrases, participial modifiers, appositive parentheticals) and can appear clause-initial or inside noun phrases, creating locally clause-like stretches that are not independent clauses.
